summary:
Players install solar panels and a battery, plan when to charge a rover, and keep the crew powered through the night. After sunrise, Scout surveys a potential building site while astronauts check the water supply and test a grow light. Players use those findings to build a greenhouse and grow a first crop.

The game addresses the challenge of making space exploration understandable through decisions and visible consequences. Children see why stored energy matters after sunset and why growing plants requires preparation. Its lessons draw on NASA resources, including Mars Trek and plant research from the Open Science Data Repository. Rover readings and resource values are simulated for gameplay.

Junior Astronaut gives children a way to explore how science and engineering help people solve practical problems in space.
details:
Junior Astronaut is a browser-based educational game where children help four astronauts build and operate a small Mars base. Players choose construction kits and locations, watch the crew assemble equipment, and plan how to store enough solar energy to power the base through the night.

After sunrise, the Scout rover surveys a site. Players then assign astronauts to check the water supply and test a grow light. These findings unlock a greenhouse, where players can grow their first crop. Each task connects a decision to a visible result, helping children explore how energy, water and research support a space mission.

The project uses a 2.5D map built with Three.js, React, Next.js and TypeScript. Zustand manages the game state. We used Bun for development and testing, and Playwright for browser checks and gameplay recording. The game includes separate 3D models of the habitat, greenhouse, astronaut and rover.

The research activities draw on NASA resources, including Mars Trek and the Open Science Data Repository. Scout’s readings, resource costs and task durations are simulations designed for the game. We also considered children’s understanding, mobile controls, reduced-motion preferences and the need to distinguish NASA research from simulated gameplay. The intended impact is to make space science and engineering approachable through exploration and problem-solving.
